utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gustafson, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And good morning, Dr. Kicanovic. If we can start by going to your statement, which is D3089, and I believe you have it in front of you. If you could look at paragraph 8 of your statement. And, Dr. Kicanovic, that paragraph, does the wording of this paragraph reflect your own words that you said to the Defence investigator, or was the wording of that paragraph suggested to you by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I believe the witness's microphone needs to be turned on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Your microphone hasn't been activated. Yes, now, it is. Could you repeat your answer kindly, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. No one suggested it to me. That's what things were like at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: By any chance was Mr. Cvijetin Simic, the former president of Bijeljina Municipal Assembly, present when you gave your statement to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't present. I was alone when I provided a statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Then if that's the case and if paragraph 8 reflects your own words, do you have any explanation for the fact that the wording in paragraph 8 of your statement appears verbatim in Mr. Cvijetin Simic's Defence witness statement? And that's 1D07803.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose it figures in his statement as well, because at the time we lived and worked in the same town, so in all likelihood, what he has to say is what I wanted to say too.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 24708 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And in fact, Dr. Kicanovic, we've done a comparison, and the language in paragraphs 5, 6, 8, and 9 of your statement appear almost verbatim in those same paragraphs of Mr. Simic's statement and that comparison is now on the screen before you. So paragraph 5 is virtually verbatim the same. There's a minor grammatical difference. Paragraph 6 is verbatim, identical to Mr. Simic's statement. As we discussed, the language in your paragraph 8 appears verbatim in his statement as well. There are some differences in capitalisation. And paragraph 9 of your statement again appears virtually verbatim in Mr. Simic's statement. Would you agree with me that if in fact these paragraphs reflect your words that you gave to the Defence investigator and if the same applies to Mr. Simic, that would be a rather extraordinary coincidence?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all likelihood you are right. They appear almost verbatim, it seems, but Mr. Cvijetin Simic and I were frequently in contact. We worked together, and on top of it all, I was their family doctor, his family doctor. Perhaps things match. Perhaps we think along the same lines, but that's what things were like. Before being contacted by Defence counsel, I did not discuss these matters with Mr. Cvijetin Simic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: How about after you were contacted by Defence counsel, did you discuss these matters with Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once, I believe, in passing. It was not an official conversation. I just mentioned that I had been contacted, and I was surprised to have been picked as a witness, a Defence witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we need translation?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I don't believe so, Your Honours. The two statements have been translated. This is just a -- more or less a visual depiction of the similarities and differences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: To understand it correctly, I would like to have a translation. We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI P6184, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. -- Dr. Kicanovic, you discussed in some detail the events in Bijeljina on the 31st of March, 1992, and the following few days, and that's at paragraphs 12 to 15 of your statement. And when I read your statement, I admit I was somewhat taken aback by the fact that there was no mention whatsoever of Arkan or Arkan's Serbian Volunteer Guard anywhere. You don't dispute, do you, that a group of Arkan's Serbian Volunteer Guard forces entered Bijeljina at this time and was involved in the conflict there?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not dispute that. However, I did not refer to it since, if you look at my statement, on the 31st of March and on the 1st of April, that night I spent guarding my building, guarding my family, wife, children, and grandchildren. Early in the morning that day, I left Bijeljina and went to the countryside where there were no upsetting events, nothing that would hint at anything evil happening. Had I -- then I left my family with my friends in the country and tried to get back to the town, believing that I could be of assistance as a surgeon. However, I was not able to enter the town due to combat. I don't know who fought whom at the time, but I returned to Dvorovi village, which is 4 kilometres away from Bijeljina, where I set up a makeshift outpatient clinic so that in case there were injuries or woundings, we could take care of the wounded, and indeed that's what happened. Early in the morning, they already brought in a number of wounded whom we treated initially and then sent on to hospitals in Serbia. As for Arkan, yes, it's a fact that he was in Bijeljina. I wasn't in Bijeljina at the time, though.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: How about when you returned to the town on the 3rd of April or on the following days? Did you see Arkan's men in the town then?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, they were about town. I didn't see them, though. But when I returned to the town, I went to the hospital. I went back on my own, since my family was in the country, and I was very busy trying to sort things out at the hospital since it had been blocked by Muslim forces. There was chaos and all of the medication was gone. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm just going to interrupt you because you did answer my question in the first line. You said you -- that Arkan's men were about town but you didn't see them. And I'd just like to ask you to limit your answer --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd just like to ask you to please limit your answers to the specific question I pose just because our time is limited. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. You said in your statement at paragraph 22 that there was no take-over of power in Bijeljina. You said that Bijeljina municipality was not overtaken but kept. But it's true, is it not, that the events of early April 1992 included a political transformation such that Bijeljina became an entity of the Bosnian Serb state or became known as Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time -- may I? At the time, Republika Srpska did not exist. There was only Bosnia and Herzegovina. At the elections, we won power in a legal way because we had the majority and we set up our authorities and the Assembly together with the Muslims. There were 18 of their deputies in the Assembly. I see no reason for the term "take-over." It simply went on as it was before. As for the Bosnian Serbs, well, that may not be the best choice of words, but then it's your choice.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we have P2629, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Dr. Kicanovic, the document that's appearing on your screen is a report from the Bijeljina Public Security Station, and in the third paragraph on the first page it states that since the 1st of April, 1992, the Bijeljina Public Security Station has existed and operated according to the instructions and guidelines of the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And it states that on the 31st of March, all contacts with the Tuzla Security Services Centre stopped, and no reports or information on the current situation have been sent to them despite daily requests to this effect sent by the old security services centre to which the Bijeljina Public Security Station belonged up to the 1st of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we go to page 2 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S. And it's at the bottom of the page in B/C/S and in the middle of the English just below the first set of underlined words.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It says: "Currently we are augmenting our reserves to meet the 100 per cent increase. I have managed to procure some of the equipment, berets and badges with the tricolour from the Serbian MUP and our police officers have worn them since they first went out into the streets on 4 April 1992." And this report indicates, does it not, that things did not simply go on as they were before, certainly not with respect to the MUP, which transformed into an entity of the Bosnian Serb Republic; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you'll have to discuss that with someone from the MUP. As I told you, I was in the health sector only. I'm not aware of this. I do know, however, that in terms of health care, all ties have been severed between us and the funds, and we remained isolated. As for any berets and badges, it's not something I can comment on. I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And were you aware that Mr. Novakovic, Bijeljina deputy at the 16th Assembly session, that's the republic Assembly, on the 12th of May, 1992, said, and this is P956, page 22: "The region of Semberija and Majevica, since what is Serbian there was liberated long ago and the people are already gradually getting used to it. I must say that those who were our enemies, in other words, the Muslims, that they got used to this, too, and interestingly, from my lifetime experience and what I have seen in the last month, they co-operate best when there is Serbian rule. That is what they react to best. When there is Serbian authority, then there is peace in the house." Now, clearly, Mr. Novakovic by describing events in Semberija and Majevica as liberation and making observations from what he has seen particularly in the past month regarding the reaction of Muslims to Serbian rule, he is not describing a situation where things went on as before, but, rather, a transformation to Serbian rule; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way he put it. He was a deputy, and those are his words. However, in Bijeljina and in Ugljevik and Lopare, which form part of Semberija and Majevica, even before these events, Serbs had power in the Assembly and Executive Boards. Muslims, I don't know what they had and what they had to get used to. They lived alongside Serbs in a loyal fashion as they do nowadays. What Dr. Novakovic had in mind when he said that is something I can't explain.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. At paragraph 27 of your statement you were asked about adjudicated facts regarding SDS activities in Bijeljina, including actions of Bijeljina Crisis Staff members, and in that paragraph you state: "There was never a Crisis Staff in Bijeljina." I'm going to put to you, Dr. Kicanovic, that that's totally false. There was an active and functioning Crisis Staff in Bijeljina at the time of the conflict there and beyond.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bijeljina was the Presidency of the Bijeljina Municipal Assembly. Because the Assembly could not be convened for a session, a municipal Presidency was set up comprising some 10 people who managed the municipality at the time. If someone called that group "Crisis Staff," that's something I am unaware of. I was not persuaded or convinced that it was a Crisis Staff. A Crisis Staff is a different thing. In Bijeljina, at first and later on into the war, no state of war was declared.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Can we go to P2629 again, please. And if we could go to the bottom of page 1 in the English and page 3 in the B/C/S. And here it says that the -- at the bottom of page 1: "During the night and the next day," and it's talking about the 31st of March, "the Territorial Defence, the Serbian National Guard and the Serbian Volunteer Guard starting removing the barricades under the supervision of the Bijeljina Municipal Assembly Crisis Staff." And if we could now go to P2626.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. Could we have some time to establish this? To find it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It's at the bottom of page 1, the top of page 2 in the English, and it's the first full paragraph on page 3 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wonder if it's legible at all. Just let's collapse the English one for the moment and zoom in.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unless there's a translation error, the document doesn't say that the barricades were controlled by the Crisis Staff. It says that these were Muslim barricades.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, but it least the witness to a wrong trap.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The English says -- it's quite clear that it says that the Serbian National Guard and the Serbian Volunteer Guard starting removing the barricades under the supervision of the Crisis Staff --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's see whether ... "Krizni Stab," is it "Crisis Staff"? Eighth line. Is that what is to be translated "Crisis Staff"?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You may take up this issue in your re-examination then. Let's continue, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes. If we could go to P2626.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is a fax from the Bijeljina Crisis Staff to the SDS Main Board reporting on the situation on the 1st of April, 1992, in Bijeljina, and you can see "Bijeljina Crisis Staff" appears both at the very top of the page and again type signed at the bottom "Crisis Staff Bijeljina." And we have in evidence as well a televised interview with Mrs. Plavsic - this is P5587 - during her visit to Bijeljina, and she says: "It was my choice to first visit the local Serbian people's Crisis Staff and meet here with Mr. Arkan and his associates."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to P2855, page 5 of the English and page 6 of the B/C/S. This is a report from the 28th of July, 1992, from the VRS Main Staff on paramilitaries, and at the bottom of the English and in the middle of the B/C/S it says: "Although they were banned, the municipal Crisis Staff in Bijeljina and individual Crisis Staffs in local communes are still functioning in the Eastern Bosnia Corps zone of responsibility." It says: "They are connected by radio and the so-called guards communications centre is also in this link. The Crisis Staffs mostly employ the guards' supporters." Now, Dr. Kicanovic, we've now seen, I think, five references to the Bijeljina Crisis Staff including a fax from that Crisis Staff to the SDS Main Board. Now, whatever you may think about the existence of this Crisis Staff, it clearly existed and functioned, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do believe that the Crisis Staff existed somewhere. However, as regards Bijeljina and its Municipal Board, I was unaware of any Crisis Staff. Secondly, you mentioned that the Crisis Staff was in control of the barricades. The barricades in Bijeljina were set up by Muslims and no Crisis Staff had anything to do with it. If there was a Muslim Crisis Staff which set up the barricades, then that's fine, but as regards the municipal leadership in Bijeljina, we only had the Presidency which functioned. Now, if someone called it "Crisis Staff" or defined as such, then, well, please. I didn't look at it as a Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. At paragraph 24 of your statement you were asked about the adjudicated fact that 48 bodies were collected from the town's streets and that 45 of those bodies were of non-Serbs. And you said that according to your findings, there were 42 casualties, 7 of whom were Serb victims. Now did you personally see any of the bodies of any of these victims?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came to the hospital I saw many bodies which were not taken care of at all according to the medical rules, and I requested from the public security station to send someone to identify those who were dead and to remove them from the hospital complex. Individually, I did not see anyone. The report was given to me by the official who conducted the on-site investigation, so that was the information that I learned, and this is what I said in my statement. As for the number of 48, I suppose that some additional persons were identified except for the information provided by the person who conducted the on-site investigation at the hospital. There were seven Serbs and the first casualty in Bijeljina was a young woman who came out onto her balcony to see what was happening and who was hit by a bullet in her chest. That's what happened at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So you don't dispute that there could have been 48 bodies collected from the streets, but your number of 42 came from an investigation conducted of the -- in relation to the bodies that were at the hospital. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. In the hospital complex, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to 65 ter 08281, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is a "Slobodna Bosna" article from the 10th of April, 1992. Now, "Slobodna Bosna," that was a Sarajevo-based publication; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in the -- if we could zoom in a little bit on the left-hand side of the B/C/S and the bold text there and then the other text to the left there describes a visit to Bijeljina by a state delegation consisting of Biljana Plavsic, Fikret Abdic, and General Prascevic. Do you recall this state delegation visiting Bijeljina in the days following the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it. That was immediately after the conflict. They first came to the town of Bijeljina, but they could not enter it because of the guards which were guarding the roads. They were not announced. The guards were not informed about their visit, and then they came on the following day and they did enter the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. If we could move to the middle of the B/C/S in that box, you see it says "The victims," and there is a list there of names in bold of victims of the conflict in Bijeljina. And I'd like you to look at that list and tell me if you can confirm, based on your knowledge, that any of those people were indeed victims as this article states.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For example, this one Lukic, it was the brother of Veljko Lukic Kurijak [phoen] who was a people's hero. And Mirjana Lukic, that was first casualty that I mentioned. As for the others, I do not recognise their names. Yes, this one Redzep, up here. I used to know him. He lost his life because they found weapons in his house. This is Zvonko. I think he was just a passer-by in the street who got killed. And as for the others, judging by the names, I really could not claim that those were the ones. Or Bego Sindric. Bego Sindric, he wasn't. He was wounded, and we found him at the Bijeljina hospital. He was in the emergency room because he had a gunshot wound to his lungs, and his gall had burst, and we treated him.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And did he survive?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He survived these events, but, no, eventually he didn't. He died several days afterwards, after all of these events.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 2 in both languages, please. Now, this is at the -- this is the first full paragraph on page 2 of the B/C/S, so on the far left-hand side, and the last paragraph under the heading on the -- in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And the journalist is describing the site when entering the town, and says that there was a Serbian flag raised on top of the mosque. Do you recall this, the Serbian flag being raised on top of the mosque after the conflict in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it was taken off quickly, it was an insult both to the Serbs and the Muslims. There was a flag, but it was an irresponsible person who put it there. And I really don't like the cartoon which is depicted here, but that's up to Mr. Ajanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And then if we go to the text just below the heading, it describes a discussion -- a meeting between Fikret Abdic and General Jankovic, and in the second paragraph General Jankovic says that there are some refugees. He says that there are 300 people --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not receiving interpretation. I mean I don't hear anything in my headphones.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: How about now? Can you hear me now? Okay. So now --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm now looking at the text just below the heading discussing the refugees, and General Jankovic says that there are about 300 people here, and he's at the barracks at that point. And that there -- but he says that there are about 1.500 in Patkovaca, and he says, "In this camp we have both Serbs and Muslims. In Patkovaca there are only the Muslims." Can you confirm that there were these refugees in these locations as described by General Jankovic here?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were refugees but I can confirm that there were many people at the barracks in Bijeljina which is a huge area. Many people came there seeking shelter from these unfortunate events, the shootouts in the town. Many people sought shelter there, and in my belief, as I saw them there, they were well taken care of. They received food and tea and so on, and they were safe there. All of them felt safe and secure in the barracks. And as for Patkovaca and this camp, I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the location Patkovaca?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the neighbouring village next to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 5 of the English and page -- this is also on page 2 of the B/C/S but on the far right-hand side. And this is about in the middle of the page, just below the middle, and it starts with a reference to the park. And it says that -- and this is the top of the English, that Biljana Plavsic, General Pascevic and General Jankovic talked to Arkan in the park. Plavsic appeals to Arkan to allow the army to take over the town. Arkan refuses. And then in the next paragraph or two paragraphs down it says: "Dr. Klicanovic came along to protest against plunder of Muslim houses and talked to a man in a grey suit apparently from the Serbian Crisis Staff. This must not go on. It must stop. And then went on to speak of the torture of a child." Now, the name is Klicanovic, but I assume that's a reference to you, and I'd like to ask you do you recall -- and I note also that in paragraph 15 of your statement you talked about the mistreatment of a Serb boy in the hospital. Do you recall making this protest about the plunder of Muslim houses and the torture of a child on this occasion when the state delegation was in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember, but once again, in the park, there is a square in front of the Bijeljina municipality building with plain trees which we called a small park in Bijeljina. It's in the centre of the town, and it's an open space. Yes. As for this, that Arkan requested to take over the barracks, he was not allowed to do that, and he did not take over it. And I remember that I directly addressed a man whose name I don't know or anything else, but I said, Please protect the Muslims, protect the people, because all this time we were receiving instructions, even from President Karadzic, that the civilians were to be treated in a humane way and that the soldiers were to be treated in accordance with the Geneva Conventions. And as for this boy whom I mentioned, it was an 11-year-old boy who was operated on because he had his appendix removed two days before these unfortunate events in Bijeljina, and they threw him out. And when his father came to pick him up, then they beat him up and they also beat up his father. So before I came here, I talked to this man who does not like to remember these events, and thank God the boy recovered well and now he's a grown-up man doing his job and so on and so forth. So I meant, when I talked about him, that all the people should be protected from those who -- to say frankly, individuals who, like anywhere in wars, were doing many things that are inappropriate for humankind and inappropriate to be done by a contemporary man.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And then just below that reference it refers to Plavsic thanking Arkan for his intervention and kissing him good-bye. And again I'd like to ask you if you recall that Mrs. Plavsic thanked Arkan and kissed him good-bye on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that she kissed him, and in addition to that, whether she thanked him or not, this is something I didn't hear it. But the journalist, I see it's Sejo Omeragic here, they used to write all sorts of things at the time. And believe me, they were the ones who fanned the flames of hatred, the inter-ethnic hatred at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, the Chamber has received evidence of a video of Mrs. Plavsic kissing Arkan good-bye that appeared on television. You didn't see this -- this kiss on television?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on TV, because at the time we did not watch TV at all. There was no electricity in Bijeljina so -- but personally I haven't seen that. I didn't see it then, and I didn't see it later, because believe me, I only watched sports on TV after everything that has happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: On the basis of the witness's answers to my questions, I'd like to tender this article.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think that the parts of the article that the witness confirmed can be admitted, and if you want to go through that, we could identify them or else I could do that with Ms. Gunderson [sic]. But there were some parts of the article he confirmed, some he didn't confirm, and most of it is not discussed at all, so we think we should be selective in how we admit it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He discussed it and I am of the view we need to admit it in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, there's a lot of portions of this article that deal with topics that he didn't discuss, and particularly it seems like it would be unfair given that you've refused to allow us to subpoena Fikret Abdic who was mentioned in many of the parts of this article, so to allow some journalist's version of these events without giving us the opportunity to -- hear from a participant seems unfair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I mean the parts that were put to the witness I certainly agreed with. The parts that weren't shown to him, that will obviously go to the weight of the article, but I believe there's sufficient indicia of reliability based on the witness's answers for this article to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will admit only those parts which were put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6185, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Dr. Kicanovic, did you have any personal interactions with Arkan during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, because I treated his fighters. He had many wounded who were brought to our hospital, and he paid to the hospital regularly, because his fighters had no insurance. So he did visit the hospital, as I say, in connection with his wounded soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So you would meet with him at the hospital; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. I saw him later on in other places, too. For example, on one occasion I met him I can't remember where. Outside the hospital. But for the most part the contact we had took place at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm a little confused. Did you meet him at the hospital during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't meet him in the sense that we had appointments, but I used to see him from time to time, and I met him in the sense that we had to resolve the problems concerning his wounded soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honours, I see that I'm just at my 45 minutes. I have one topic. It should take five to seven minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Dr. Kicanovic, at paragraphs 25 to 27 of your statement, you commented on some adjudicated facts relating to expulsions and other crimes against Muslims from Bijeljina, and at paragraph 25, sorry, you assert that there was no organised campaign of looting and expulsions targeting Bijeljina Muslims. It's true, is it not, that thousands of Muslims from Bijeljina were expelled during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miss, if a thousand Muslims had been expelled from Bijeljina, I cannot claim that it wasn't so, but they were not expelled. They left. They went away from the area where combat was ongoing and where the Muslims were no longer a majority. However, as I said, there were individual attempts to take the Muslims over across the demarcation line. In any case, lists were received from Tuzla listing people who should be taken over. This was done by individuals. It had nothing to do with the authorities in Bijeljina. There were no expulsions whatsoever. After all, there were Muslims working in my hospital. They worked there during the war and they continue to do so now. So no one expelled them. And as for the fact that they left, they did. Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I understand it's your position that there were no expulsions although people left.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to P54 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there weren't.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: P5483, please. This is an ICRC press release. It's only in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I will read the relevant part to you. It says: "On the night of 28 August," and this is 1994, "a group of 432 Muslims from the Bijeljina area were forced by Bosnian Serb authorities to cross the front line into Bosnian government held territory near the town of Tuzla. This was the eighth such transfer since mid-July, bringing to 1.102 the number of Muslim civilians driven out of the area."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could now go to P5423, and page -- on page 2 there is a protest letter to Dr. Karadzic, again only in English, dated the 20th of September, 1994. Mr. Akashi conveys his utter dismay at the fact that in the past few days, over 2.500 Muslim civilians have been forcibly expelled from the area of Bijeljina and Janja. It says many of those vulnerable people expelled were apparently robbed and abused en route by criminal elements led by a man known as Vojkan. And then it refers to assurances that Dr. Karadzic had given that such expulsions were not in accordance with Bosnian Serb policies, and then describes the failure to -- Akashi's failure to understand how this deplorable situation could continue despite these commitments.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And the Chamber's received as well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now, your question, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have a couple more -- one more document to show the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was wondering the point of you putting these documents after your time is up. You asked the question and the witness answered. You can use this in your final submission.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, no, I'm now trying to impeach the witness and my goal is to show him a number of documents that will show that everybody knew this and that he must have known it too. And I would just like to show him one more document in that regard and then put my question if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Dr. Kicanovic, if we could now go to P1473. And I will mention as well that the Chamber has received into evidence a UN Security Council Resolution complaining about the ethnic cleansing in Bijeljina at this time - and that's P5424 - and a BBC television report on Vojkan's ethnic cleansing activities, P2073.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go now go to page 87 of this document in both languages. This is an extract from General Mladic's military notebook from the 13th of April, 1995, and the heading is "Meeting with the parents of prisoners." And Mr. Djordje Krstic says to General Mladic: It is not clear to us who orders the expulsion of Muslims. Vojkan takes them away in their socks. Djordje Sekulic, further down the page, says the rumour in Bijeljina is that Mauzer is taking away Muslims and not Vojkan. On the next page, Dragica Spasojevic says: The persecution of the Muslims will make the position of our children worse, and she's referring to Serb prisoners. And Zorica Stjepanovic says: There are groups that are doing incredible things, that Vojkan does strange things. Now, Dr. Kicanovic, the ICRC knew, the UN knew, Dr. Karadzic knew, General Mladic knew, and these apparently ordinary inhabitants of Bijeljina knew that Muslims were being expelled from Bijeljina. This information was widely disseminated to the public. You must have known this, too; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Expulsions. Vojkan Djurkovic, Vojislav Djurkovic, Vojislav Puskar, did these kind of things during the war. He did take the Muslims up to the demarcation line but not in the sense of expelling them, but in the sense of helping them to leave the territory. These people are living around the world nowadays. They probably requested to go somewhere where they would live better, but no one talks here about the multitude of Serbs who had come from the towns which were under Muslim control, from Tuzla and including Zenica, Sarajevo, Bugojno, and so on and so forth. All the big towns. At the hospital I --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Dr. Kicanovic, I'm sorry to interrupt you, but your answer is now straying away from the question. Thank you for answering my --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I think he should be allowed to complete his answer. She's already used up more than enough time. The least she can do is give him a little time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Kicanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. At the time I was the director of the hospital, and I received 280 members of medical staff who left other towns. Were they expelled or whether they came to Bijeljina because they would feel better there, I don't know, but it was the same with the Muslims. No one expelled them. No one forced them away. They went where life would be better for them. Those who wanted to stay stayed and they could work normally. Even at the Bijeljina hospital we had two doctors who were Muslims and who continued to work throughout the war. So it was not a matter of expulsions but simply, as I say, helping people to go where they wanted to go. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Kicanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, if you have any re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only a few questions, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Kicanovic.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to remind you yet again to pause as I do myself and to speak slowly. On page 3 you were asked about some terms or linguistic formulations used in your statement. Can you tell us who took your statement and who took Mr. Simic's statement, if you know who he discussed it with? You don't need to mention the name, but is it the same investigator?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Leaving aside the words themselves, what about the gist of what you shared with us in the statement? Is what you said objectively true?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think it is absolutely true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 5 you were asked what country there existed on the 31st of March and the 1st of April, or what state. Can you tell us in what capacity did Biljana Plavsic, Fikret Abdic and others visit Bijeljina during the crisis?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They visited it as members of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as members of the Presidency. Since the Presidency comprised five people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you recall until what date we recognised the existence of the central authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably until the Assembly. I don't know. When did they set up the referendum to secede, because the Serbs did not wish to leave Yugoslavia in order to unite -- to join the unitary Bosnia-Herzegovina. I don't know about a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So on the 1st and 2nd of April, Biljana Plavsic still participated in the work of the joint bodies.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And she was there with Doko and Fikret in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at P2629. No, 2626, please. 2629. Let's save time, then. 2629, then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see anything.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll deal with it. Page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First of all, in the middle of paragraph 3, because it's illegible, I'm going to read it out. For the sake of caution, the Crisis Staff of the SAO Bijeljina decided to renew the work of elementary schools and so on. How does this tally with your ideas of the existence of a staff and Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is what is in dispute here. You see, there is a reference here to the Presidency, that the Crisis Staff grew into the Presidency. No. The Presidency was established from the list of Assemblymen of the municipality of Bijeljina and some other persons. The Presidency of the Municipal Assembly existed and it was in charge of life in Bijeljina, the reconstruction of schools, bringing power, water, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll go back to that. Let us look at paragraph 2, where it has been suggested that barricades were placed under the control of the Crisis Staff. I would like to read this carefully and ask the interpreters --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry. That was never suggested. I simply read out this passage that says that the National Guard and the Serbian Volunteer Guard started removing the barricades under the supervision of the Bijeljina Crisis Staff. So there was never any suggestion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- that the barricades were under the control of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Correct. Shall we locate the paragraph first.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's on the page that we see. It's the second page from the top in Serbian, and it's probably the removal of barricades. Actually it starts on the previous page in English, most probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson never talked about the issue of barricade was control of who. It was you that raised the question by way of intervention. Do you refer to the paragraph starting with "The removal of barricades"?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. It's the previous one. Then that's the interpretation I received, and I believe that the witness intervened as well, saying that it wasn't the Crisis Staff that put up these barricades. Then probably the interpretation into Serbian was poor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could help us, Ms. Gustafson, in finding the B/C/S paragraph. Do we see it in front of us now?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It should be in the middle of page 3 of the B/C/S. I'm not sure what page we're on now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the English paragraph is the one we are seeing in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's right, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Starting with "The removal of barricades ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, the -- it starts on the preceding page, but that's it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Shall we show the first page. Let's read out -- let the witness read out the full paragraph. Now, what is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is whether this police report sent to Minister Stanisic here correctly states that the Crisis Staff grew into the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You clarified that a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Second question: The Territorial Defence, was it a legitimate formation in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in Bijeljina there was only the Territorial Defence. As far as legal formations are concerned, these were people who were territorials and who had prepared earlier on for possible -- well, you know yourself what Territorial Defence means.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That was probably a mistranslation or misinterpretation of what the learned Ms. Gustafson said. It turned out that it was the Crisis Staff that controlled the barricades. All right. We can drop that now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have P2629 in order to clarify this confusion regarding Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Kicanovic, do you make a distinction between party organs and state organs?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P2629. I beg your pardon. 2626. I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Party organs, did they have executive power in the municipality or could they just report to the party, inform the party?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Party organs could report to the party and individuals took part in government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We had a better one, but all right, we see it in English. Please, can you tell us here on the basis of the letterhead -- I'm going to read it out in English because it's more legible. The SDS of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the SDS Municipal Board Bijeljina Crisis Staff to SDS Main Board Sarajevo. Subject, yes, report. Now, this Crisis Staff of the party, is that the same thing as the Crisis Staff of the municipal authorities?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not the same thing. The party was separate then, and of course now parties are also separate from government. They participate to the extent to which they participate in government as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now go back to that document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then, Dr. Kicanovic, do you then confirm there existed a Crisis Staff in SDS Bijeljina? Bijeljina SDS.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Probably that did exist. I was not involved because I had other commitments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us -- let us not call up that article. It's already been admitted. Can you tell us, Lukic, Mirjana Ilic, Lazarevic, Djokic, Novakovic and others, what is their ethnic background? And they are among the victims.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course they're Serbs, ethnic Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were asked about that I think on page 9, or was it 8? It's that text from "Slobodna Bosna" where the names of the victims are mentioned, and you noticed these names?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then you advocated the protection of Muslims, and you spoke against the looting of Muslim houses.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could all unnecessary microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is the ethnic background of this young boy who was mistreated in hospital and who was it that mistreated him?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name is Dragan Kalabic. His ethnic background is Serb and he was mistreated by the Muslims who had occupied the hospital and who put up barricades in front of the hospital preventing anyone else except for them from entering the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It doesn't say who it was that mistreated him. It wasn't all the Muslims; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not all the Muslims, but the extremists who entered the hospital. I don't know the exact names of the persons who entered the hospital and I didn't ask who they were exactly, but at any rate, it was the extremist Muslims who had started the war in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 19, you mentioned that some Muslims stayed on living in Bijeljina and that there were some who worked in hospital throughout the war and that they still work there today. Can you tell us what the differentia specifica is? What was the distinction between those who wanted to stay and those who wanted to leave?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the difference or distinction is, but those who wanted to stay stayed and probably felt safe. Probably those who were afraid of something left. So what would happen would be that during one night we would have no more Muslim nurses left because they had simply left the hospital, and there was no pressure that had been exerted whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Kicanovic, I would just like to mention a number D1438. We don't have to call it up. We just want the participants to see this. On the 8th of April, 1992, there is this order banning the carrying of weapons in public places, and it was Cvijetin Simic who signed it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, we did not catch the office that this person held.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How does this fit into your knowledge regarding the existence of a Crisis Staff as a municipal organ of government?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a reference here to the municipal Presidency and Mr. Cvijetin Simic who signed it. I remember that an order was issued --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow this. Without watching the document, how can the witness answer the question at all? It's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just asking -- I'm telling the participants that already this -- I mean, it was on the 8th of April that this order was issued and it was issued by the Presidency, not by the Crisis Staff. But we can take a look at it, D1438.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who was not allowed to carry weapons and who issued this order?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everyone was prohibited from carrying long-barrelled weapons in the street, because there was truly chaos there. And this was issued by the Presidency of the municipality, and it was Mr. Cvijetin Simic who was the president of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what the date was and how this tallies with your own position regarding the existence of a Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the date is. You said it was the 8th of April. I cannot see it here because I simply cannot see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. I see. Presidency of the Municipal Assembly of Bijeljina, for the president Cvijetin Simic, the date is the 8th of April, 1992, and that has nothing to do with the Crisis Staff. That is the Presidency of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who would have signed this order had there been a Crisis Staff in existence at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably the person who was in charge of the Crisis Staff, and there -- that was not Cvijetin Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked about the departure of -- actually, you saw or we saw that in some documents there's a reference to the forcible expulsion of Muslims. Can you tell us how big a unit would have to be in order to expel 2.500 Muslims and what unit would that be?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was not a single unit that did that. There were individuals. In order for someone to expel 2.500 persons, he'd probably have to have a well-armed unit. I don't know. I'm not very knowledgeable about these things, but say 400 men? But that did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Vojkan, how many armed soldiers did he have who would have carried out that expulsion?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vojkan Djurkovic did not have any soldiers. He just had this friend, a pal who helped him, and again, I'm saying that he did that on the basis of lists that were submitted to him from Tuzla through a certain Mr. Bakir Pasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This Bakir Pasic, what was his ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't know his ethnic background, but in terms of religious background he must have been a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber what the position of the authorities was, central and local, in relation to the departure of persons on any basis, the departure of Muslims from Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one at any level was in favour of having people leave their homes, so an effort was made to have everyone stay at home. For a variety of reasons that did not happen, and then Muslims were moved to Muslim territories and Serbs to Serb territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know what my position was regarding people's departures on any basis and also in terms of return? What was my position?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was very familiar with your position. Your position was absolutely, absolutely, first of all, against the war; and secondly, persons who are autochthonous should stay where they were. Very often you said the war will pass and we have to stay on here and live together with each other.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D473. Could I have that in e-court, please, briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was there any risks involved in returns before the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Bijeljina or anywhere?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Anywhere. On the whole, was returning before the war was over a risky business?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. I think that it was risky. And if people -- well, I'm not sure there were any excesses in Bijeljina as regards returns. For example, Janja, that is part of the municipality of Bijeljina, practically everybody returned, and they moved back to their own property.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a summary from the working meeting, MUP -- in the MUP on the 20th of August, 1992. In English page 10, in Serbian page 8, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In English it says "The situation in Bijeljina," and in Serbian it says: "The situation in Bijeljina is relatively satisfactory, but in truth it is much worse than at first glance. The problem with the Muslim section of the population is compounded by the arrival of Muslim refugees and the return of those who had left Bijeljina before. And it was Mr. Karadzic's and Mr. Panic's recent statements that influenced this. The population includes a number of Muslim extremists, and it is believed that a large number of Muslim citizens owned weapons." Do you remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry. The witness has absolutely no connection to this document, and this is a leading way of putting the question. If Dr. Karadzic wants to ask a question about events at this time, he should just ask it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic asked the witness about his own position at the time and the problem of returning refugees, and on that basis probably Mr. Karadzic can ask the witness whether it's consistent with his observation in a neutral way, not in a leading way. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Kicanovic, how does this tally with your knowledge of my positions concerning returns even during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, during the war the number of returns was reduced. Of course, since a large number of Serbs arrived in Bijeljina who were refugees themselves, and now we had Muslims returning to Bijeljina who had fled before, and there were possibilities of conflict. However, I had no knowledge of any incidents on those grounds. Quite the other way around. People exchanged apartments and houses as in the best friendly relationships. It was your position that everyone should stay on their own, and if there are movements, that everyone should be adequately compensated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was it also made part of the Dayton Accords? In other words, whoever did not want to return had to be compensated?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE KICANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Kicanovic. I have no further questions. Thank you for everything you did for all three peoples.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you as well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kicanovic -- oh. Can we upload that document. According to this paragraph, the return of Muslim refugees was influenced by Mr. Karadzic's speech. Do you remember what that speech was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise, but I truly don't remember. I don't know where that speech took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's fine. Unless my colleagues have a question for you, that concludes your evidence, Dr. Kicanovic. On behalf of this Chamber, I thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Would the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sarenac. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you start giving your evidence, Mr. Sarenac, I must draw your attention to a certain Rule that we have here at the International Tribunal. That is Rule 90(E) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Under this Rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled in such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sarenac. Do you hear me? Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Lieutenant-Colonel Sarenac.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Kindly speak slowly, which also applies to me, and kindly pause between questions and answers so as to have everything recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Given the fact that your testimony will be led live without your statement being tendered, kindly tell us when and where you were born, and what your first and last name is as well as your father's name.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: I was -- my name is Desimir Sarenac, father's name Novica. I was born on the 5th of May, 1948, in Stari Brod village, Rogatica municipality, Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Briefly enumerate the degrees you have or your educational background.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: I completed primary school in Borike, Rogatica municipality. I completed the secondary military school in Sarajevo in 1968. I completed the military academy in 1982.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us more about your movements in terms of military service and what were your positions?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: My first position was in Delnice, the Republic of Croatia, between 1968 and 1972. As of 1972 until 1977, I worked in Zagreb as platoon commander. I was platoon commander in Delnice as well as in Zagreb. In 1973, in Zagreb, I joined the military security service. I remained with the service throughout my military career. In 1977, I was transferred to the Bihac garrison as required by the needs of the military. I had the duty of the office -- security officer there. In 1982, I was transferred from Bihac to the Gospic garrison in Croatia where my position was that of security officer until September 1990. In September 1990, I was transferred to the Belgrade garrison as part of regular procedure to the position of security officer as well. I remained in Belgrade until mid-May 1992, when I was transferred to Sarajevo to the 49th Brigade of the JNA or its 4th Corps. I was also security officer there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll continue with where you left it off. Can you just tell us in the meantime something about the period of your active-duty service in the JNA. Were you commended or did you receive certain awards?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Yes, I was both commended and received awards during my service with the JNA. I have of the medal for military service and two decorations, one for military service in the JNA with the silver swords, and the medal for the service to the people with service swords. I was also decorated in the VRS where I received the medal for the service to the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the situation like on the 16th of May, in mid-May, that is, 1992, when you arrived in the 4th JNA Corps in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: On the 16th of May, I arrived in the corps where I was appointed security officer in the 49th Brigade. That was the unit's name at the time. The situation was such in the units that officers and soldiers who were then still in the JNA awaited their return to their places of birth in Serbia and other republics. Both the officers and soldiers who hailed from Bosnia-Herzegovina, like myself, remained there or were preparing themselves to remain with the units. Once those soldiers and officers from Serbia and other republics left, the unit was practically decimated. For a while, and especially since I was a new person in the unit, I was very disoriented and very worried as to what the future might hold in store, by which time there had already been attacks on JNA units. There was the pogrom on the JNA column leaving Sarajevo on the 3rd of May. Then there was the case in Tuzla, on the 15th of May, where soldiers were killed en route out of Tuzla. As for the 49th Brigade, eight soldiers went missing on the 22nd of April. All of that had an impact on the morale and sentiments of the personnel which remained. It was a very uneasy situation to be in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the time of your arrival, did you already know anything about the fate of the eight missing soldiers?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: A search was still under way, and all measures had been taken through the organs in Sarajevo, because at that time the JNA was still the legal -- the lawful force in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the army command at the time still operated in its peacetime location in Bistrik. However, there was no verified information as to their whereabouts. There was only speculation as to what could have happened with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about later? Was it ever found out what had happened to them?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Later on we received information, but although it wasn't final information because there were different versions in circulation, that they were taken to the old boiler room in the settlement of Srakino Selo and their throats were slit. Another version had it that they were killed in a park next to the department store Sarajevo. Another version had it that they were killed in another park at Bjelave. So for the most part, throughout the war, the search continued much like it continued for other people who went missing, although no final conclusion was ever reached as to their fate and their mortal remains were never found.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us something about the situation in Lukavica, where you were, and what was your relationship like with the neighbouring Serb and Muslim civilian population?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: As of mid-May, from when I arrived until, say, mid-June, I was trying to acquaint myself with the location. The barracks served also as a reception centre for refugees from Sarajevo and its environs such as Visoko and other parts and villages where people were under threat. They all came there where accommodation was found for them. In the barracks there was a mess, and at some point, perhaps a month after my arrival, someone recognised a group of Muslim civilians who came to the mess buying food for themselves. They came from Dobrinja. As it turned out, it happened to have been a daily occurrence. They came regularly, and they had the possibility of -- come and purchase goods. Immediately adjacent to the barracks there were Muslim families living there who remained throughout the war. Not all of them, of course. Some of them in the meantime wanted to go elsewhere. They went to Sarajevo and elsewhere, be it on their own or in a different way. Some asked for help as well, whereas others left of their own accord.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was your relationship like with those Muslim neighbours?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: As an officer of the JNA, I did not look upon those people in any other way other than their being civilian. I did not distinguish between them and Serbs. They were always safe, even after they were introduced to me. On one such occasion -- well, my brother Cedo was killed on the 28th of May, 1993, at Sjemec, near Rogatica. A few days later, since I attended his funeral, I returned. There was a workers' platoon where there were Serbs and local Muslims who took upon themselves to do some jobs like bringing in material to a certain location or to put up a wall. For the most part they didn't have to dig anything, but they would build a wall here and there. And when I toured the working unit, I distributed cigarettes to them since it was a rare commodity, especially for those soldiers who smoked. And since there were Serbs and Muslims there, later on I heard from Vojo Vukotic who was there that Alija Viteskic had a comment to make. He said, "I thought he would kill us all," because he knew I had just attended my brother's funeral. When they saw me, they expected my reaction. However, as it turned out, I simply greeted them and distributed cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the Serbs and the Muslims who were not conscripted -- under a work obligation?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Yes. The Serbs equally as the Muslims were under the work obligation, and it consisted in meeting some of our needs when something was necessary to be done in the barracks, perhaps, for example, to set up curtains or to lay out blankets or camouflage nets or some other curtains that would shield us from sniper fire, because we were shot at by snipers in all areas that were visibly -- that were visible, that were open to view within the barracks. So our main task was to make a good protection that would shield us from reconnaissance, observation, and sniper attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did the Muslims have to serve the army, and were they members of the Army of Republika Srpska and on what basis?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: That was a voluntary matter. They were not mobilised. For example, we had a neighbour from the Dedic family - I would rather not mention his first name - who volunteered of his own free will, and up until mid-1993 or so, he was in the Army of Republika Srpska. Later on he expressed a wish to go abroad and he left. And there were those who remained in the Army of Republika Srpska throughout the war, like, for example, one Muric. Once again I would rather not mention his first name if I do not have to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any Croats in the command and in the units?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Well, in my particular command we did not have a Croat. There was one in the corps, one Solar who used to be an officer there as I remember. As for Croats, there were some Croats among the soldiers, but I could not remember any specific names. I know for sure, however, that there were some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You came to the 49th Mechanised Brigade. After the withdrawal of the JNA and the establishment of the Army of Republika Srpska and the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, what happened with this unit?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: The 49th Brigade was renamed and it became the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade. As the troops had been decimated, the unit was now manned by conscripts who had fled Sarajevo and other surrounding places and other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, from Zenica all the way to Kakanj and other areas from Central Bosnia. The brigade was manned with these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we call -- when we call up a map, we'll ask you to show us the zone of responsibility. Did you remain in the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade throughout the war, and which duty did you hold?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Yes, I remained in the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade throughout the war. In the position at the Slavisa Vajner-Cica barracks. That was my micro-location. And my duty was chief of security in the brigade. That was up until around the 10th of May, 1995, when for a short while I was appointed commander of the 4th Battalion in Pale or, rather, in Trebevic, because the battalion was deployed on Mount Trebevic. That was the Pale battalion which then became a part of our brigade and I was immediately appointed commander. I remained in this position from May until October 1995, when I returned once again to the command of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade to the position of chief of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us briefly how did you move through the service later on? What did you do after the Dayton Agreement?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: After the Dayton Agreement a reorganisation took place. The Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade and the corps were disbanded. There were transfers within the Army of Republika Srpska so that I was transferred with other members of the brigade command to Pale. After that, some of our officers were assigned to the then 7th Corps that was the Hercegovina Corps, and we were sent to the command of the 7th Corps in Trebinje or, rather, Lastva, where the seat of the 7th Corps was situated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Up until when did you serve in the army or, rather, worked in the armed forces? What did you do later?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: I remained in the Army of Republika Srpska up until the end of 1996. And then as there was a possibility to state my wish, whether I would remain or not, I said what was on my mind, and I went back to Belgrade to the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us what was your main duty in the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: In the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade, as a security officer, I was the only professional officer. I did not find any other personnel who had been trained to do the work. So first of all, I had to select the staff from the soldiers or reserve officers and see who would work, who would be members of my team. Our main duty was to collect information about the enemy forces and to protect the unit from intelligence or sabotage attempts and, of course, to protect it from an armed attack by enemy forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During your service, did you come in contact with representatives of UNPROFOR and other UN agencies, and what were your relations like?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Yes. Throughout the war we had contacts UNPROFOR representatives, and as the most senior officer in the -- from the command who was in the barracks, because others from the command were at a different location, I had an obligation to do that. The UNPROFOR officers regularly came to visit me, and they interviewed me about certain issues which were topical at the time. With the implementation of the Dayton Agreement, as part of the OSCE, I was a member of a delegation of officers from the Army of Republika Srpska which, in accordance with this programme, went to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We made exchanges, exchange visits as they were called at the time, visits, checks. These were mutual checks or controls.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for the OSCE which accepted you in this mission, did they run a check of your personality and your conduct during the war?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Well, we had to receive -- all of us officers who were in this team, we had to have the approval of the government of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and their command, the command of their army. We had to be accepted by them, because obviously they ran checks to see which people they could accept, who was acceptable for them, in other words. So I know that I passed. Otherwise, I couldn't have been a member of the team, and they wouldn't have accepted me.
