utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In what ways did you collect the information which you used to protect your unit from enemy attacks?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: The soldiers of our unit, the units of our army and the Muslim army were continually in touch from the beginning of the war. Sometimes they even shared rooms in one and the same building. You have a building where there would be a crew from the Muslim army and a crew from the Serbian Army in a different room. So the basic fact was this direct touch. Then there were people leaving Sarajevo all the time. They had been mobilised members of the Muslim army or people who were not members of the army who had been hiding and evading mobilisation and who then defected to our territory. We would interview them and collect information about the deployment, the forces, combat equipment that the Muslim army had at its disposal so that we would know what and whom we were facing and how we could protect ourselves and prepare for our defence. In addition to this, of course, we forwarded the information to the corps security and intelligence organ which, through their interception activities and their own intelligence checks, checked all the information that we forwarded to them. We also exchanged information with the organs of specific units, other brigades of the Army of Republika Srpska, which made up the corps. So we would compare the data, and what would be the use of data or information that was unverified? No one would do anything with such information that was not verified or checked because that would mean nothing. One of the verifications concerned the combat activities that the Muslim forces were carrying out. Then we would check the specific locations, the size of certain formations that were deployed there and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber what was the main duty of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and what was its strategy as opposed to the strategy of the 1st Corps of the Muslim army? From the point of view of your brigade and from what you knew.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Our main task was to protect the positions that we had taken control of, the positions on which we already were. In order to protect the depth of our territory, the rear, where the Serb-populated settlements were located and where the Serbian people lived, because if we had not managed to do that, there would certainly be no guarantees that we would have survived on the left bank of the Drina at all, because the forces of the 1st Corps of the Muslim army which were engaged with us, my brigade and the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps as a whole, continually exerted pressure, carried out combat activities and were moving lines to our damage with the goal to take over these areas and have full control over them as complete masters. If the lines had broken, if they had been broken through, and if our defence had been broken down and if the Muslim army could have advanced as much as it wanted to, then certainly we could not have stopped before reaching the Drina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned to us that you had direct touch with the enemy side throughout the war. Can you tell us about the whole of the corps, as far as you know, what were the forces of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina that you were engaged with directly?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: As for the potential of the Muslim army, they had huge potential in terms of troops. There were so many people in Sarajevo that they could mobilise. Facing my brigade we had three Muslim brigades. They made a ring around the Muslim-populated part of Sarajevo, and they were facing us. That was the way they were deployed. In addition to these three Muslim brigades which were opposed to us, not counting the numerous forces of the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior and other special forces which were not part of the composition of these brigades but were stationed in the combat deployment of the Muslim forces. They were a part of it. In addition to these three brigades facing my brigade, there were a number of other brigades as well, including the 2nd Mountain Brigade, the 1st and 2nd Motorised Brigades, then the Independent Kosevo Battalion, the 2nd Chivalrous, then the 102nd, later the 105th which was formed, and this is just a part of the brigades. If the Muslims said in their media during the war and especially after the war that they had 120.000 armed combatants in the city, then you can imagine what sort of force that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And as for contact with other corps, can you tell us anything about that? Not your brigade but the corps as a whole.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: You mean the corps including the brigades. The units of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, the contact that they had with other brigades, if I understood you properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With other corps of the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Yes, with the Zenica corps in the direction of the Nisici plateau and then with the units of -- which were stationed in Gorazde. So in fact, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was surrounded from the inside and also from the back, if that was what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us something about the use of artillery of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps? Or, rather, generally, can you tell us about the tactics and the interest of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps? Actually, in the indictment and in certain statements, claims are made that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps used artillery indiscriminately against the city and even for the purposes of terror. Can you tell us what the interest and the tactic and the strategy of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was in terms of the city itself?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: From my position that I had, that is to say, what I knew, generally speaking, the use of artillery and shells in a built-up area has no effect. That is just a waste, a squandering of resources, if you will. I know that there were responses to fire, artillery fire that had come in, so artillery fire was responded to by artillery fire against the points from where that artillery fire had come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have any information about what the 1st Corps had, the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, later on the 12th Division, in the city itself, what kind of firing positions and firing points and potentials they had?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: We did have information, but then, of course, it comes time and again, so from day one there was not a single day when somebody did not leave Sarajevo, especially persons who had been mobilised into the Muslim army. As a matter of fact, we had information about personnel, the names of commanders and others, and quite simply, we could complete personnel files about all these persons. These were in part former JNA officers, so we knew each other from before, and now they held certain positions. They were brigade commanders like Bejic, Lutic [phoen] and others. Also, they had howitzers, long-range guns, mortars from 60, 82, and 120 millimetres respectively that were stationed at Hum, Mojmilo. In the combat disposition of these lower calibres or lower-ranking units, multiple-rocket launchers, we suffered fire from these multiple-rocket launchers from Mojmilo. Then anti-armour equipment, Maljutkas, cannons, et cetera. Tanks, they had tanks. Also, tanks were positioned in the area of Hum, in the area of Velesici and other positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me. Can I intervene one minute. Mr. Sarenac, a minute ago you told us that the use of artillery and shells has no effect in a built-up area or the -- I would quote exactly what you said. "From my position that I had, that is to say, what I knew, generally speaking, the use of artillery and shells in a built-up area has no effect." Could you expand why it is so and tell us what you exactly meant by a "built-up area"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. In buildings, in settlements, because we received so many shells from Mojmilo when our portions were targeted, 82-millimetre mortars, mortar shells. When they fall on roof tiles, it's only the roof tiles that burst, nothing else. Then perhaps a 120-millimetre shell would reach a ceiling. So if those weapons are used, then it is only roofs that break. But one has to be very skilful. It would have to be laser guided so that an artillery shell would fall somewhere into the street or onto a square. That would have to be laser guided, but that was not possible. Given the equipment that existed there, that was not possible with that kind of equipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Continuing alone the lines of His Excellency Judge Kwon's question, you said that you suffered fire from these firing positions. What is the effect of that? Where were their positions? Did you have any information about that and could you see the fire?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: We had information where the positions was -- positions were, and then when they fired, then this mortar fire would be identified. Also, if it came from long-range equipment, also they needed to have a proper area, like the area of Hum most often and the area from Hum towards Velesici, that part, where it was less populated or unpopulated, where there are forests, meadows, or where there are areas that are sparsely populated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The transcript does not reflect that the Lieutenant-Colonel said that we had information about these positions from the observers as well.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: From observation points, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us abandon this topic now. Just tell us what the position of the corps command and brigade commands was with regard to firing with heavy-calibre weapons at the city itself, apart from responding to this fire from firing positions, what were the orders and what was the general stance?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: I cannot give a specific answer because I was not kept abreast of this planning. I just know what -- well, I didn't really know about artillery very much either. I just know what its effects are. So I know -- I was not an eyewitness of the targeting of facilities, civilian zones. I don't have knowledge of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have knowledge to the effect that such orders were issued or that there were bans?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Veljko Stojanovic, my commander, was an excellent officer, very strict. I know him directly as brigade commander and he prohibited the opening of fire even from small arms apart from the command in any way, especially not to open fire from artillery weapons. And we mainly had mortars for immediate support and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The transcript did not say where artillery fire should be opened. My command, you say, did not allow the opening artillery fire against?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Without an order, without an order. Without an exclusive order from the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The brigade command or some superior command, did it ever issue an order to fire at civilian buildings or was anyone allowed that possibility?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: I am not aware of such orders that -- or I'm not aware that fire was opened at such targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now show us on the map - 1D7849, could that be called up, please? - could you mark the area of responsibility of your brigade on this map, and then could you explain to us what it is that is marked on this map and who marked that and what that depicts? 1D7849. While we're waiting, Colonel, can you tell us what this conversation with persons who fled from Sarajevo included?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Well, first they were interviewed about the motive, why they left. Also, what their status was in Sarajevo at that moment, whether they had been mobilised or not. Also family details and the situation in town, the situation of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or, rather, the situation in the units of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina that they had been mobilised into if they had been mobilised. Also their knowledge about the deployment of combat resources, technical equipment, the disposition of units, personnel, who was on the command of various units, the situation in Sarajevo, the conditions, the livings conditions, the attitude towards Serbs, because already in the beginning of the war, a discriminatory attitude was taken against the Serbs. It was sufficient to find a mirror in a Serb's apartment when such an apartment would be searched, and then this person would be accused of signalling the Serbs when it is that they can open fire and so on. And so on and so forth. When such information was received about the enemy forces and their disposition, this was compared to what was already known, and then it was checked through the corps and their organs, and there was an exchange of information with other commands, brigades of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How accurate were these statements when you cross-referenced them with other information? How correct was this information that was received during these interviews?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: From the beginning of 1992 onwards, I -- I had the opportunity, actually, in the beginning of last year, to obtain a number of documents that we worked on and it turned out that the successive documents relied on the basic information that we had first received. It was only the personnel details about persons who were members of the command or who were deployed elsewhere in a unit. Sniper shooters were identified in 1992, and these sniper shooters were known as individuals throughout the war. They stayed on, and they operated the very same way in 1992, 1994, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you exchange information with state security as well and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters not hear the rest of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a fact that we were linked to the state security, so at the same time they received copies of our findings and our notes about the deployment of enemy forces. From them we also received information about the deployment of enemy forces that they had received.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While we're waiting for the map to be uploaded, can you tell us what the ethnic background was of the persons who fled to the Serb side in the area of responsibility of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Well, most of them were Serb civilians and soldiers who had been mobilised. Then next in terms of numbers were Croats and then Muslims. That is to say, it wasn't that many Muslims who fled, but there were some. There were tens of them who defected as members of the Muslim army and came to our territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the procedure involved with these defectors of Croat and Muslim ethnic backgrounds, both civilians and soldiers?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Since -- after the interview would be carried out, after their details would be taken, they would stay on certain premises with our own soldiers. They were there so that they would resolve their status, because Croats in particular immediately wanted to go to Croatia, and they sought that possibility, to have transit to take the shortest route to Croatia. Muslims individually wanted to go abroad, whereas others towards the end of the war in particular returned to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about those who returned to Sarajevo towards the end of the war? How long did they stay with you?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps up to 30 days. As things were being cleared up and the end of it all seemed near, they probably changed their minds. Although they had originally intended to go abroad, they returned, and there was no special procedure applied on our side to allow their return.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were civilians and soldiers treated in the same way? In other words, did you treat soldiers as POWs?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: In my unit I did not have any POWs, nor did we treat these people as POWs. They could move about freely inside the barracks perimeter as our soldiers could. We all ate the same food, starting with the officers down to the soldiers and these people as well. As regards this topic, I recall an interesting detail. Their documents were deposited with me in my office, and a fortnight later, two Muslims came to see me, saying that in their notebook there was a note of 100 German marks. I was quite embarrassed or put in an uneasy situation, because other people from my team could access those documents, and I thought that someone could be tempted, if they found it, to take it. However, when we went through their notepads, we indeed found the 100 German marks, and it was worth more than anything I did previously, because things turned out that way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what's going on with e-court. Can I ask for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would advise you to move on to another topic. I'm told that the size of the file is too big, so it's very difficult to upload it. I saw it emerging, but it does not appear on our monitor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask then that the map be placed on the ELMO and we could ask Lieutenant-Colonel Sarenac to tell us what is indicated and perhaps make additional indications based on his knowledge from the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we do this exercise with -- with a somewhat more compressed one which can be offered by the Prosecution or the already existing map?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the Prosecution would be so kind as to assist, it would be very nice. We asked for their assistance when we were scanning documents, but none was received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By the way, but I noticed there are already some marks made by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, the witness has marked on this map. But it's -- each of us seem to be able to have it on our own e-courts, so I don't know, maybe if we could use the ELMO for his purposes, the rest of us can follow either with both the ELMO and on our own e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The problem is that I cannot turn it around --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I was trying -- I was trying to do that myself but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- but it's just not moving. But do you have it in hard copy, the marked map? Why don't you go on with it so we can -- why don't you show it to the Prosecution first and let's put it on the ELMO. Any observation, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I can just have a look at this, and just for the record, the request about scanning documents was whether or not we had an A1 scanner and we don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I see things on this map that weren't visible when we were looking at the image yesterday, and they tend to be pencil marks. And I may have some comment or objections as we move on with respect to the map, but I don't see why we couldn't just see how it plays out for now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. Let's put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be assisted by raising the map so as to see the lower part and the area of responsibility. So it shouldn't go up but down. [In English] Could it be lifted little bit more. More, please, to see the line, the [overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, once we place it, we can -- we could play with the machine. But let's continue, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, can you tell us what we can see in this part of the map regarding the area of responsibility of your brigade and the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: I'd like to start from one end of the map, from the beginning to the left. There you can see the positions of the 15th Mountain -- or Motorised Brigade as it was called later. It used to be the 10th Brigade. It used to be commanded by Musan Topalovic Caco. Its AOR stretched from Lapisnica, where their adjacent unit was the 2nd Mountain Brigade, via Colina Kapa, Zlatiste, Vrbanja, the Jewish Cemetery, and Borak. Next, the 101st Motorised Brigade, being one of the strongest motorised brigades, that part where the two units met was in the central part --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Sarenac. Can we do this after the lunch break so that the Judges could have a copy of that map, and then we can put the map on the panel and the witness could explain a bit more easily.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And Mr. Reid will be able to do his technological magic and come up with what you had asked for in a few more seconds as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think this is the last area that we intended to cover with this witness, so perhaps we could take our lunch break early and come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's do that. Shall we resume at 1.00? Very well. We'll have a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told that now the map is on the e-court, and we have it as well on the easel.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Excellency. Could we zoom in on the part covered by the southern marked line, the southern part of town and the area of responsibility along the line. That's good. I think it's enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, who drew the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: I did. And I put in the symbols.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do not touch the screen, please. You will be provided instructions. Do not touch the screen unless you are intending to make a marking. Thank you. Can you tell us on what basis did you mark the confrontation line and the deployment of pieces in your AOR?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Based on the information I had. I spent a number of years along that line, and it all remains vividly in my memory. I've also reminded myself only recently of it. That is why I was able to reconstruct the position of these elements. Perhaps I was off by a couple of dozen metres, but this is what it was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have the key which you drafted, and it was sent by e-mail to the participants. Perhaps we'll also need to put the key in hard copy on the ELMO because it contains all the symbols. Is this an extensive map, a comprehensive one, or did you only mark the bare minimum?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Of course it is not exhaustive because the size is small and there were many symbols to be marked. This is just a portion of the assets. However, the areas of respective units are complete. Any data on combat assets and workshops for the manufacturing of weapons are only designated partially.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you indicate a workshop or manufacturer of weapons? Didn't you mark it with a T?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Yes. There's a T in a square. It means workshop or factory. It is in Pofalici in Velesici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's the one -- or what is marked by the flags?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Seats of commands and staffs. This is Cengic Vila, and the construction company Vranica where the Main Staff was headquartered. Here in Svrakino Selo, that is the Victor Bubanj barracks. It was the headquarters of the 105th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, sir, did you wish to add anything -- or, sorry, first of all, did you indicate the weapons, staffs, and firing positions in the AORs of other brigades of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Yes, the part up there to Velesici and to the north. However, it is all relative as it is a small area. They could equally engage our positions too, but they belonged to the 1st Motorised Brigade and its command was in Buca Potok. However, its assets were in Hum. They had howitzers, mortars, tanks, and other assets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you trying to say that the forces on one side of Sarajevo supported their own forces across town on the other side?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Yes. I also indicated Strela, which is a missile. They also had tri-barrelled guns. They had weapons mounted on trucks such as mortars, anti-aircraft guns.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we can remove the key now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Sarenac, you seem to have forgotten the advice Mr. Karadzic gave you. Please put a pause between the question and answer. Please wait until the interpretation is completed before you start giving evidence. Can we see the second page of English?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is part of the key.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. If you could tell us, which you will see in a minute, what LAS, OBL, VP means. You said they are special military units.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were you asking me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are special military units. There's Lasta, for example. That's the military police. Then the unit which protected facilities and persons. It was dislocated since they were numerous. There were also signs to combat dispositions of other units for reinforcement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. What is an LAS? Or LAS? I can understand VP means military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the next page, Lieutenant-Colonel. You can have a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we provide it to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can collapse the map if necessary. Dr. Karadzic said he's over with this map.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not over. I'm not done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 2 it says "LAS" in a circle?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Lasta. It is the acronym for the Lasta special unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And next one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Headed by Vikic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And next one, OBL?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the unit for protection of buildings and persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, would you like to keep that red markings on this map?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Excellency. I would kindly ask the Lieutenant-Colonel to mark anything in addition he may have wanted to. So perhaps we can remove the key from the screen so as to have the entire map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, is there anything else you would wanted to --

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm just now looking at it but nothing comes to mind right now. I can't see it all too well. Yes, there's nothing. The basic things I wanted to are there. There are some things that are not here. For example, I wrote a T in Alipasino Polje which is the wire factory. That's where weapons were produced. First I used a normal pencil, and I left those markings in pencil, and then later on I wrote in pen over it. That is why occasionally you will see some pencil markings with numbers or letters belonging to particular units. That's why you have the pencil markings. I didn't even realise it was left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you put a circle around the T and place a number so that we have it in the transcript as to what exactly it means.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just place a 1 next to it, a red 1.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What does it depict?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: The factory where mortar shells were being produced as well as shells for other assets. It's a factory where they put the charge in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there anything else that you wanted to mark in red? Was there anything in Pofalici where they carried out refurbishment of assets?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: There was one in Pofalici, in Velesici.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Karadzic has suggested the answer to the witness quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have documents. We can bring them up if necessary, documents that this witness drafted, statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's a separate matter, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, kindly feel free to make any markings or put in numbers telling us what they are. Of course, provided you know for certain that they were there within your AOR, in terms of weapons, pieces, units, anything you deem necessary. Just place a number and tell us what it is. You don't need to put in any symbols --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I don't see any point. If we zoom out we can see the T marking marked by this witness which seems to be a factory. So there's no point of asking him now to mark it again while he's not able to see it clearly now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Excellency, however I'm not asking him to repeat but to make new markings for things he hasn't marked thus far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Forget the current marking. Why don't we zoom in further. Let's show the witness the T mark which he made probably by pencil. Zoom in further. Do you see the T mark you made? So that's the factory you referred to, Mr. Sarenac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. The wire factory. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we admit it. We can admit it as it is now, the map marked by this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour, but it's not a full map. The witness said that there were quite a few things that he did not mark within his AOR plus the other AORs, but this suffices in terms of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. If you'd like the witness to mark further places, we need to admit this one and then you can ask to make more markings and we admit it separately. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I'd actually just like on the record that I do challenge the accuracy of the markings on the map, particularly because I'm not clear whether we're proceeding on the basis of the witness's recollection or on the basis of his memory refreshed by documents that we questioned earlier on in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably that may be the area you can take up in your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So shall we give the number for this map.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's 65 ter number 24723 which is Exhibit D3091.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But that number applies to the whole of the map, not just this section of it. Very well. Can we have the entire map back, please, and zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, based on the documents you had and your knowledge, is there anything else within your brigade AOR that you would like to mark now? Just place, for example, the number 2 and tell us what it is and go on.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Well, at this point I'm really not concentrated enough to add anything, save for what I can see that is still in pencil. There is Hum where a howitzer position was as well as rocket position. That is marked already. There, there was the command of the 2nd Mountain Brigade. There's nothing else right now. I'm not focused enough. I can't add anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Lieutenant-Colonel. We will not use the map anymore, then, in that case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will the key be put under the same number as the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was presented as the English translation. Do you have any objection to that matter, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, did you have information, verified information, about the conduct of the units of the 1st Corps in the town itself regarding their own civilians and facilities?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Through gathering -- the gathering of intelligence about units and their activities, we also learned that in certain cases they shelled certain facilities in order to have it portrayed as if the Serb forces had done it. One of --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it looks like a new area that we actually have no notice for, wasn't in the previous statement, and hasn't been received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 32. Paragraph 32.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, we'll see. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And 33 also. If the witness could please be allowed to continue and to complete his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We received information, there were even some instances because they made some makeshift shells and weapons that were not tested, and it happened that they targeted our positions but as the projectiles were unsuccessful, it happened that they fell on their own facilities, so accidentally it sometimes happened that their projectiles exploded on their positions or in the civilian-populated zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to these accidental shots at their own territory because the weaponry didn't work properly, were there any deliberate attempts to do that in order to accuse the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Instances of shelling have been commented a lot. I mean, shelling people who were queueing for bread or standing in line to get water in Vase Miskina Street and later on at Markale. People on the ground were convinced at first that it was certainly not the Serbian forces that had done that, and in my view, it was only logical because this took place in a small space, small tight areas. For a mortar or artillery shell to reach such a position, it would have to be laser guided to hit such a spot. So -- and we also came by information, which I cannot cite now because I don't have them, that there were some deaths --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I think you have answered the question. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's also a completely new area, Your Honour, and I may want to cross-examine on this new area related to the specific incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, in paragraph 33 of the statement it says: "In order to involve the international community as a side in the conflict, the Muslim forces fired at civilian zones in order to accuse the Serbian side of having committed crimes." So I don't see what's new about that. This is falling directly within that topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see in e-court 1D28734.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, I will ask you to show us in this example how you worked and how you obtained intelligence. Can you please tell us what we see here.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: We see an official note dated the 4th of March, 1995, as I can see. Yes. Yes. This is about --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please have a look at the names down here in the first paragraph, can you please read out the names for us?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Yes. Of the names listed here, Rato Raseta, Faik Ibrahimagic, and Mithat Krivosic were killed in 1993 during the Bajram holiday because of an explosion of a shell in the yard of the Orthodox church near the Bristol Hotel. Officially they said that the shell came from Lukavica, but according to Kostic's claim, it's 100 per cent certain that it came from the direction of the centre of the city and that Muslims had fired it in the direction of Grbavica and that it had dropped early and fallen on their territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How does that fit with other information that you had about this? Would this be an exception or how does it fit with the other information you had?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Of course it wasn't an exception. We had a lot of information not only about shells but also about sniper fire fired by Muslims within the city. They would -- shot at people from snipers, especially women in mourning were their targets, because the women of Serbian ethnicity who are mourning someone are wearing black clothes, and therefore they were clear targets. There were also squarings of accounts among them. If they were rivals, they would use this to eliminate those who were against them so they would no longer be bothered by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As for this Radovan Uljarevic, can you tell us who that was and who was Kostic?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Radovan Uljarevic was an officer from my security organ, and Kostic was a defector. He had fled the Muslim territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3092, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, after the incidents for which the Serbs were blamed, did you run any checks in your brigade in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps? Did you check the allegations of such accusations, and if so, how?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Well, we would examine whether any fire was launched from our positions through commanders including the battalion commanders who were at the front line. And we knew ourselves, because the commands, both the corps command and the brigade commands were perhaps 200 to 500 metres at the most from the front line. So the commands could directly monitor the fire. They were not very far away. One of the cases in which we ran a check, we had complaints from UNPROFOR that a French UNPROFOR soldier had been killed at an observation point located at the Jewish Cemetery. UNPROFOR officers arrived first to lodge a protest, and then they requested that we should tour our positions together with them, and I was assigned to go to this tour. The French soldier was killed at the Jewish Cemetery which is uphill from our positions and it was not visible. There are obstructions. Simply, our positions were downhill from there so they could see for themselves that it was not possible that he was killed by our sniper fire, but, rather, certainly by Muslim sniper fire. That was one of the incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Lieutenant-Colonel, sir, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I just have your indulgence for a moment, Your Honours, to speak with Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. What I was just discussing with Mr. Tieger was what might be the most appropriate course of action I could bring to Your Honours' attention given the extremely late notice of the map, the new information that we've just received with respect to the scheduled incidents, and of course, the comments with respect to one document which was one of the 230 questioned documents. So I would ask Your Honours this if I may: There are certainly some areas I -- and I'm prepared to begin my cross-examination on a number of areas, but I would ask Your Honours' indulgence to be able to conclude the cross-examination tomorrow morning so that I could have a chance to investigate these two new areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we don't oppose that. That seems reasonable, but I would like to add that we offered to bring the next witness in advance of this witness because of the map and the Prosecution declined, so -- but in any event, we don't mind if they complete as much of the cross-examination as they can today and then continue -- wrap it up tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or we may hear your cross-examination tomorrow, instead we proceed with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't have the next witness here because we expected this cross-examination would take up the whole day. And also we won't finish all the witnesses this week if we don't use the time with this witness right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's unfortunate. I will consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well, Ms. Edgerton. We'll see how far you could go and see what -- what we can do afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, and my apologies. It was in light of new information that came later on today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I said how far you could go. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, do you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one thing I'd like to deal with that you mentioned in your evidence to Dr. Karadzic earlier today. You said that between -- from May to October 1995, you had become -- or were appointed the commander of the 4th Battalion of your brigade, the 1st Sarajevo Motorised Brigade. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you describe to us your battalion's area of responsibility throughout that period?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: The zone of responsibility of the battalion which I commanded between May and October 1995 extended from Lapisnica -- or, rather, the quarry close to Kozija Cuprija, Lapisnica. Then Trebevic where the funicular was and where some of the Olympic facilities were, such as the sled run and so on. Through Zvjezdarnica on Trebevic, all the way to the point where we linked up with the 2nd Battalion of my brigade and that was in the Zlatiste sector on Mount Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps we could look at a cutout from a map, given the description you've just given us.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And it's 65 ter number 08191J. It's a cutout, Your Honours, from P848. And of course we only need one version, and could you zoom in on it. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you see, Lieutenant-Colonel, the designation on the far right-hand corner of this map cutout in Cyrillic preceded by the number 4. Could you tell us what that abbreviation means?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: This is the 4th Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Now, if you look, Lieutenant-Colonel, at the -- the lines between the 1st Brigade and this 4th Brigade, does that roughly correspond with your area of responsibility as you've just described to us.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Well, this 4th Battalion which I've just identified was part of the composition of the brigade but it is not depicted here in such a way that I could connect it properly. Could we please zoom in a little bit into this area where the 4th is so that I can see the area. As it is now I cannot identify it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could just zoom in a little bit more. I think the Lieutenant-Colonel wants to see if he can recognise place names and they're a bit illegible. And if you could scroll this zoom over so that it heads to the western part of Sarajevo. And then could you scroll it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If this is okay with you, Lieutenant-Colonel, could you scroll it up so we see the northern area exposed. Do you recognise your battalion's area of responsibility, Lieutenant-Colonel, and if not, we'll move on?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: No. This was not my battalion's zone, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. We'll just move on. Now, just to clarify one more thing, is it correct that you were based at Lukavica throughout the conflict, Lieutenant-Colonel?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Yes. I was deployed in Lukavica throughout the conflict except for this one period, but that was under the command of the same brigade because I was the battalion commander then.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In fact, you -- it seems like you exercised an additional function at Lukavica at least for a period. You were also barracks commander, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: One could say so. I said that recently. I said that as the most senior officer in the barracks, I was responsible for law and order under the wartime conditions, and that included construction repairs because of damage caused by shelling, and I had to organise these repairs as well. But this was no special function. In addition to that, I had nothing special to do, nor did I have any obligation to organise work and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: As senior -- the most senior officer in the barracks, were you responsible for monitoring movement in and out of the compound?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, I was responsible for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So given that, you would be able to confirm an event on 22nd June 1992, the arrival of almost 300 detainees from Hadzici who were bused to the Cica barracks on that day?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That was what happened. I was ordered to prepare space for them and to secure them. Practically I had no other contact with them. I engaged my police to accommodate these people on the premises of buildings in the barracks. They were accommodated on one of the floors in rooms where soldiers had been saying previously. As far as I remember, they stayed there perhaps only for one night. I'm not sure if they stayed any longer. In the same manner they came for them and took them away, and I had no authority over them, nor did I have any other obligations concerning them than to accommodate them there and secure them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And could you just tell us, based on your knowledge, who brought them, if you recall, and who took them away?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, and I cannot be completely sure anymore, they came escorted by the civilian police who secured them. They were handed over to us. Certainly it was not military security but civilian security. They delivered them to us, we accommodated them, but as I told you, I think that on the following day immediately they had gone. They left. They just spent the night there and then they were transported away, but I cannot remember now who were the persons. I just remember the event.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Would you be in a position to remember from which opstina, which municipality, these civilian police authorities had come from?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: I don't know, believe me. At the time, I was still a newcomer. It had only been a month, and I didn't really know anybody there yet, but I just know that these people from Hadzici were there, from the area of Hadzici. That's what I was told.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And now actually I would like to go over to -- or return to the map that we had discussed earlier, that you discussed earlier in your examination-in-chief with Dr. Karadzic, and I just have to remind myself of the exhibit number. Your indulgence for a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3091, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. If we could have D3092 up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And before getting into some detail about the map, I'd just like to ask you one question. You said in your evidence that you had reminded yourself recently on the state of affairs as it was during the conflict. And could you tell us how you reminded yourself?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: I reminded myself because I got hold of documents. I had documents before me. That's what jogged my memory. I had forgotten all of it. It's been 20 years. Of course, when that happened, I asked a certain institution for access to these documents, because how useful would my testimony here be if I were trying to remember and if I were guessing.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the institution that you asked for access to these documents, was that the RS state archive in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, the state archive.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, did you go get those documents yourself or did someone go collect them for you?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: No, I did not go myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And who went to go and collect the documents for you?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: From the Defence team. Savcic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you remember this Mr. Savcic's first name?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: I can only guess now. Was it Milomir? I don't know. I cannot remember. I didn't know him personally up until a year ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you tell this Mr. Savcic where in the archives to go and look?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know in which section it was. Anyway, I assumed that it was supposed to be there. I asked, because I don't have the material resources to go to Banja Luka. It's far away from me. So he looked it up there. Now, where, how, I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. So you didn't tell him what to go and look for either, did you?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Well, of course, I said to him the documents that have to do with my activity, the documents that I worked on, if they do exist there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And were those the documents that you had a look at after you arrived here at The Hague?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Well, these were documents -- these were part of the documents. However, there are more documents. However, these are part of the documents that exist, so simply the documents that were made available.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And those didn't only come from the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade, did they?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Well, not the ones I saw, but perhaps that's not even 5 per cent that weren't from there, but these were important documents that came from the intelligence organ of the Main Staff and from the intelligence organ of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and also from state security. And I mean the security officers of other brigades, like the Ilidza Brigade, the Vogosca Brigade, and I mean the centre of public security that also dealt with this subject matter and investigated, gave information about the combat disposition of the Muslim forces, their combat equipment and activities, and certain persons who were identified as sniper shooters or persons who had committed other crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in all those documents that you reviewed, you didn't see a single one where you were actually the operative who was recording the interview, did you?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Well, yes. There are several documents here that I authored. I interviewed persons -- or in the case when I did not interview persons, I then wrote up information on the basis of the interviews conducted by my operatives and the notes taken by them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that's exactly the extent of the documents that you yourself authored, Lieutenant-Colonel, isn't it? That was -- those were the documents where you did not interview the persons, but you wrote up the information on the basis of interviews conducted by your operatives; correct?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Well, there is less information of that kind, that I compiled that way. Most of this consists of my notes that I personally wrote up on the basis of my own interviews with the persons who had come over. My experience with these persons who came over, first I would talk to them briefly, and then I would send such a person to an operative who would interview him. And then, of course, after that, after the note was written up and after the report was written up by the person who had fled, then I got the most basic information out and compiled an analysis. So I dealt with this analytically, what we did know already, what we did not know, what is being confirmed or not. That was the aim of this information, to see what is confirmed and what is not. So that this information would go in the briefest form possible to the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps or, rather, the intelligence organ, intelligence and security organ who would then, on the basis of that, take appropriate measures, reconnaissance, interception, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. We'll come back to that because now we have the map in front of us, and I want to ask you a couple of specific questions about this map. But so that you're better able to deal with my questions --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I wonder if we could have a zoom in on the area of Dobrinja, so that's just north of the airport on this map. Great. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now I see you marked confrontation lines on -- in this area, in Dobrinja. So what actually did you base those markings that you've made here on?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: These lines, well, on the basis of information previously known and information that is contained in our documents, on the basis of which I compiled my entire statement and so on. Here, in Dobrinja, of course, I did not have the opportunity, I did not have the resources to clearly delineate this laser sharp. This is, I mean, a schematic that is supposed to show the positions. I cannot claim that I exactly went through this building here. That is -- I mean, otherwise, if somebody were to ask me now, I could not say, well, it's not that way, it's 200 metres here, or 200 metres there, or 500 metres there. This is not a topographic map where they have these precise elements and so on, and it's not that I can orient myself that way. So this is a city map, and on the basis of that, I could do that. I mean, I was compelled to do it that way because, in a way, it was acceptable to the degree it can be acceptable and I think it is acceptable that is what the disposition was.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well -- so you drew this line then, as I understand what you're saying, based on information that was previously known and information that's contained in your documents, and you've already given evidence that you checked that information that was contained in the documents. You checked that information for accuracy. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Of course I checked. Of course. And what I was sure of, I presented here.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Could we -- I'd like to show you, actually, another cutout from a map of Dobrinja. It's 65 ter number 09390C, page 16, and it's a cutout from P00815, and it depicts the confrontation lines between your forces and 1st Corps forces as of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment, please. I've just asked Mr. Reid to do something that would help the Lieutenant-Colonel answer the next question that I'm going to ask him. If I could have your indulgence, he says it would take him one second to do. No, a couple of minutes, so we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, the front lines as shown in this area of Dobrinja are actually 500 metres further south-east than what you drew them. It seems like the information you were relying on was actually incorrect, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: If you allow me, as far as I can see the line here, likewise. I'm sure that the line did not extend this way. Who made this? Well, I'd put that question to the person who made this line, because this is not the way the line went. You can see that almost all of Dobrinja was held by the forces of the 1st Corps but that was not actually the case. It's just part of the buildings here. Our forces were deeper in the neighbourhood of Dobrinja here. I see Bijelo Polje as well, that that is being included. However, Bijelo Polje has to be -- I mean, rather, the line has to be further to the east. So this map is -- well, I understand it's -- I mean, in order to find your way and to be able to talk on this basis, I just see that this map does not reflect the actual state of affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, still on the subject of Dobrinja, we will go to another map, and it's P01739, and it's a map, General -- Lieutenant-Colonel, which depicts the locations of a number of shelling and sniping incidents in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: There shouldn't be any problem with the size of this one. That's page number 10 in the Prosecution's Sarajevo map book.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Lieutenant-Colonel, if you have a look at the map in front of you, you see -- you can see the same area that you sketched the front line on in your map that you prepared yesterday afternoon. The dot, the green dot that you see here that's number 4, Lieutenant-Colonel, is the scene of the incident where the football game shelling took place that you referred to in your testimony earlier today. Lieutenant-Colonel, if the map that you drew is accurate, that shelling incident would have taken place in Bosnian Serb-held territory. Do you still stand by the marked map that you made?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: I do apologise. I cannot see this number 4, the dot that is number 4. In red I see 3, 6, and 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Number 4 is in green. And it's immediately to the right of number 6.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Yes. I see the number 4 now, but the colour is different. It's dark. I told you a moment ago, when I did my drawing, I didn't have precise information. Well, perhaps in respect of the building but I did not have precise information. This just served as -- I mean, it is a fact as far as the zones of responsibility are concerned, the boundaries of one brigade and another brigade in depth, in depth. Now, it is only natural after 20 years that I cannot find it in my memory exactly, because this was an interrupted line, and we shared certain buildings, Muslim crews and Serb crews, and there was not a line of that kind. So I allow for that what you've said. I'm not claiming that I drew a straight line as far as the depth is concerned. However, as far as the direction is concerned and the brigade existing there, it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. If we could go back to the map you marked, P3092, I'd like to look at another area.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Please tell me I've got the number right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have some difficulty, technical difficulty with the courtroom computer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Normally it's me who transposes the numbers of exhibits and 65 ter numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So while we are waiting, Mr. Robinson, could you tell me about the witness list for this week?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The next witness is Mane Djuric and his cross-examination is 1 hour and 15 minutes, and the one after that is Slavoljub Mladjenovic who is slated for a one-hour cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would have had two more areas to deal with on this map which shouldn't have taken time and then just a short bit about the new information today. I'm in Your Honours' hands as to how to proceed. Perhaps we can see if this is fixable within the very short term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us see.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I have a couple of paper copies of this map, but I don't know how the Lieutenant-Colonel feels, but I think it's really quite difficult to discern markings on the paper copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On the map you showed to the witness just now, i.e., Exhibit P1739, the 500 metre would be tantamount about 5 to 6 metres -- 6 centimetres on that map. But what's the scale of the A1 map which was produced by the Defence? Do you have it, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, I don't, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's the city map. We can take a look at the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think it's 1:20000 on Mr. Robinson's map.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: 1 centimetre equals 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's 1:20000. So the map we saw in the binder was 1:12500. So it's about half the size.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My sincere apologies for my mathematical errors yet again. I'm in Your Honours' hands. If we were to continue this tomorrow, I anticipate it would be very brief, probably half an hour, and if we continue to have computer problems, what I could probably do is have enlarged paper cutouts of the portions of the map I'd like to ask the Lieutenant-Colonel about prepared. I really -- I don't want to waste everybody's time waiting for something that might not be fixable in the short term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Then I will consult my colleagues first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So given the circumstances, the Chamber will rise for today, and tomorrow we would like to exhaust all the witness list tomorrow so it may become necessary to have some extended sitting a little bit. Before we adjourn, there's a small administrative matter I'd like to deal with, Mr. Robinson. And in assessing the accused's motion to admit documents previously marked for identification which was filed 21st of February, 2013, we have noted that four of the documents referred to in that motion contain significant portions which are illegible, rendering the English translation of these documents also incomplete. So they are MFI D2511, D2564, D2565, and D2566. I would therefore like you to look into whether you have more legible copies of these documents, and if so, to upload them to e-court and to inform the Chamber as such by next week, i.e., Wednesday, 13th of March, 2013. And please liaise with the Prosecution in locating copies if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll do that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now we can see the map, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I actually can't yet. Wonderful.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to look -- I'm sorry, Lieutenant-Colonel. Thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to look at the area of Bjelave on this map which, Madam Registrar, is in the -- on the right-hand side of the map, far right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And do you see -- do you see the place name Bjelave marked just to the left of --

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, what exactly, could you tell us, did you mean to mark at -- by your blue markings? This area?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: The light artillery battery -- the light artillery battalion was located here. It had machine-guns and anti-aircraft weapons as well. They were accommodated at the dentistry school where training was also taking place. And this unit LARD PVO, which is the light artillery battalion, was attached to the 1st Motorised Brigade as necessary or any other brigade if there was a need. It depended on the combat situation and the operations that were ongoing.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Now, this answer that you've just given, what did you -- what do you base that on?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Well, there are several bases, but one of the fighters who had defected and crossed over to us was a member of this light artillery battalion. First he completed his training there and then he remained a member of this unit until he was -- he -- the conditions had been created for him to leave. So this is one of the pieces of information that we had. But, of course, information was checked. It's not the one and only, but I say we had one fighter who was there in the composition of this unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you've just said -- now this information that you've checked, you've just said that they were accommodated at the dentistry school. You mean the school for dental technicians in Bjelave; correct?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you actually even know where that is?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you see, you put the map here. As for Sarajevo, I have forgotten many things. This is the old part of Sarajevo which I used to know somewhat better, but now I cannot -- and considering the size of the symbols, I had to depict it as I have. I could not have found the school and then show it as a school, but textually and verbally I tried to explain it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. So you didn't know, then, that the school is actually on Cekalusa Street, at Cekalusa - and I apologise for my mispronunciation - Cekalusa, number 84, did you?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Well, I did not take this into consideration now. When we collected information we collected that, too, but when I was preparing to draw in these symbols, of course I didn't have that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the information whether that's the new name or the old one. Because even I don't know. I have lived for 50 years in Sarajevo and I'm not aware of Cekalusa.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could -- perhaps we could even zoom in a bit on -- actually I'll help my colleague. Madam Registrar, if we could call up 65 ter number 24720, we can show you actually where Cekalusa Street is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, do you see, Lieutenant-Colonel, that Cekalusa Street starts just off Bolnicka, which is to the right of the St. Mihovil cemetery and runs down to join up with Dzidzikovac Street and further towards Mejtas. Do you see Cekalusa there?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: I have to a little bit --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you see the red cross on the --

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: On top? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if you follow Bolnicka Street down from the red cross, Cekalusa Street branches off from that just at the intersection where you see the sign for medical faculty. Cekalusa Street where the dental technician school is located is actually completely the other side of Bjelave where you marked it as being.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Well, I tried to orient myself by the toponym, by the name Bjelave, and as for the map, I did not have the overview at the time to put it right there. I said that I -- I'm not claiming anything different. I'm just saying that it was in the medical school, but the symbols were not shown in the exact positions. I'm not sure if that changes anything, because obviously they were there. Now as for the fact that the symbol is not corresponding but textually and the fact that they were there ...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, what it changes, actually, is the reliability of the markings that you've made, Lieutenant-Colonel, despite your best efforts, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR SARENAC
utterances.text: Well, you could say that for the markings, but as for the fact that they were there, I still claim that it was checked and verified that that was indeed where they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Lieutenant-Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The version we are seeing now is one that is blown up.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It is. And I would like, if I could, Your Honours, because it's so much easier to see, to have that marked as a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6186, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And then that concludes my cross-examination, I think, with respect to the map, Your Honours. If I could now have your indulgence to finish the rest of it tomorrow morning. I anticipate, as I said, it would be half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Sarenac, we will adjourn for today and continue tomorrow morning. I'd like to advise you not to discuss with anybody else about your testimony while you're giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have understood. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The hearing is adjourned.
